newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: South Pacific ends nuclear rift with France.
newsitem.headline: South Pacific ends nuclear rift with France.

text.p: The South Pacific Forum on Thursday readmitted France as a dialogue partner, prompting a French minister to make a hurried trip to the remote Marshall Islands for weekend talks with Pacific island states.
The 16-nation group ended their rift with Paris over its nuclear tests in French Polynesia, agreeing France's readmission take effect immediately.

"Leaders look forward to the resumption and further development of constructive relationship at a regional level with France," the Pacific leaders said in a statement at the end of their three-day meeting in the Marshall Islands.
Post-forum talks start on Friday and end on Sunday. French European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier is expected to arrive in the Marshall Islands on Saturday, a Forum official said.
France was suspended from the forum last year in protest at its final series of nuclear tests in French Polynesia between September 1995 and January this year.

"The suspension imposed after (forum) dialogue talks last year has been a significant and effective part of the region's campaign against nuclear testing," the leaders said in the statement, which was received in Sydney.

The South Pacific Forum decided to lift the suspension in light of France's permanent cessation of testing, its signing of the South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty in March and its support for a Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT).
But while the Pacific states have forgiven France over its nuclear testing, it has not forgotten the issue.
The forum will ask Barnier to commit Paris to long-term responsibility for any damage caused at its nuclear test sites of Mururoa and Fangataufu atolls, an official said.
Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan said France would be asked to step up monitoring of its contaminated sites.

"We want them to be inside the ring so we can tell them exactly of the concerns of the countries close to the testing ground, to make them responsible for any damages at all, whether here now or into the future," Chan told reporters.
"The speed of their movement, I hope, will be translated into the speed of their interest in this region and the speed to the conformity of some of the requests we hope to ask them."
In their final communique the Pacific leaders called for environmental damage to be covered by a civil nuclear liability scheme now being negotiated by the International Atomic Energy Agency.

The leaders also called for all U.N. members to sign the CTBT. Australia plans to introduce a resolution at the U.N. General Assembly starting on September 9 calling for the stalled CTBT to be voted on, despite opposition by India.
New Delhi, which exploded a nuclear device in 1974 but has denied possessing atomic weapons, says the treaty is flawed.
The Pacific leaders said they "expected members to take the lead in the United Nations by early co-sponsorship of the CTBT resolution".

But the leaders backed away from a call by Papua New Guinea to extend the South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty to ban the shipment of nuclear weapons through the region, referring the plan to a committee for a report.

The annual forum brings together leaders from Australia, the Cook Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, Fiji, Kiribati, Marshall Islands, Nauru, New Zealand, Niue, Palau, Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, Vanuatu and Western Samoa.
